content:
<Rep. Richard E. Neal>: Committee Democrats oppose H.R. 9722, Fair Treatment of Religious Organizations Act of 2026. This bill does nothing to address the affordability crisis or bring relief to families struggling under the weight of higher health care bills, pain at the pump, or rising grocery costs. The Majority would rather manufacture problems involving charities and unions than stand up to the President, root out corruption, and lower costs for constituents. The Committee could have marked up legislation to revoke his tax immunity agreement, dissolve the ballroom project, or turn off the President's trade-related price hikes, if only the Majority would stiffen their spines.
Religious freedom is an American bedrock value that all of us support and is protected by the First Amendment. However, this bill would allow religious tax-exempt organizations to obtain and preserve federal tax benefits while espousing deeply harmful or discriminatory beliefs. This bill prohibits the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) from denying tax-exempt status to a religious organization even if its beliefs or practices on marriage, sexuality, or gender identity are inconsistent with law or public policy. It also provides that a belief cannot fail to be a religious purpose simply because it is not central or compelled by a particular religion.
This bill would permanently exempt religious organizations from the Section 501(c)(3) public policy requirement when it comes to their practices concerning marriage, sexuality, and gender identity--no matter how egregious those actions are. For instance, this would apply to practices related to same-sex marriage, interracial marriage, polygamous marriage, and child marriages. This bill would prevent the IRS from withholding tax-exempt status to a group that invents a belief tomorrow purely to discriminate, with no grounding in religious tradition.
This bill is essentially repealing the Supreme Court case, Bob Jones University v. United States, 461 U.S. 574 (1983). Over 40 years ago, the Supreme Court affirmed that Americans should not be forced to subsidize an organization whose core practices violate fundamental public policy or promote illegal conduct. In Bob Jones University, the organization claimed that its religious beliefs permitted it to reject any student who is married to a person of a different race. The Supreme Court held that the organization was entitled to its religious belief, but it is not entitled to require taxpayers to subsidize a practice contrary to law or public policy.
By exempting practices concerning sexuality from the public policy test, this bill would force the IRS to approve tax-exempt status for a church whose tenets support child pornography or sex between children and adults. In 2010, the United States Tax Court affirmed the IRS's decision denying tax exempt status to an organization whose stated purpose was to decriminalize sex between adults and children and eviscerate our child pornography laws because the purpose was contrary to public policy and promoted criminal conduct. This bill inhibits the public policy doctrine and strips this tool away for anything labeled as a religious belief about sexuality, giving bad actors a roadmap for wrongdoing.
Committee Democrats offered several commonsense amendments to exempt conduct contrary to law and public policy from the bill:
• An amendment to exclude from the bill any
``belief or practice'' that discriminates against same-
sex marriage, promotes polygamy or marriage to minors,
promotes exploitation or endangerment of children, or
discriminates based on gender identity or sexual
orientation. Failed on party-line vote.
• An amendment to exclude from the bill any
``belief or practice'' that promotes the marriage of
children under 18. Failed on party-line vote.
• An amendment to exclude from the bill any
``belief or practice'' that promotes female genital
mutilation. Failed on party-line vote.
This bill would set a dangerous precedent. It would provide a permanent taxpayer-funded license to discriminate or act against law and public policy.
For these reasons, we oppose this bill.
Sincerely,
Richard E. Neal,
Ranking Member.
